title: Making a floating media unit from plywood
subtitle: Build a hollow plywood box cabinet, fix it to the wall on a cleat, and fit a shelf inside for AV equipment and storage
excerpt: How to build a wall-hung floating media unit from 18 mm plywood. Covers designing the box, cutting and assembling the carcase, locating wall fixings, hanging the unit, and fitting the front detail.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade joinery and cabinet-making practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: The structural box of a cabinet: the top, bottom, sides, and back panels assembled together as a rigid unit before any face frame, doors, or shelves are fitted. For a wall-hung unit, the carcase is fixed to a wall cleat via a french cleat or screwed directly through the back panel into wall fixings.

A wall-fixing system using two interlocking bevelled timber pieces. One piece is fixed to the wall with the bevel facing up and out; a matching piece with the bevel facing down is fixed to the back of the cabinet. The cabinet hooks over the wall piece, bearing the weight through the interlock. Allows the unit to be slid to adjust position and lifted off without removing fixings.

content.text: A floating media unit is a wall-hung plywood box that houses AV equipment, cables, and storage with no visible legs. The
is built as a hollow box, fixed through the back to the wall, with a shelf inside and an open or door-covered face. INTERMEDIATE: accurate box-making and a secure wall-fixing are the two key skills.

Plan the external dimensions to suit the wall space. A standard media unit is 1200 to 1500 mm wide, 300 to 400 mm deep, and 200 to 250 mm tall. Decide the height above the floor for comfortable viewing. Allow cable holes through the back panel to the wall for power and HDMI. Cut the parts list: two side panels, top and bottom panels, a back panel, one mid shelf, and a face strip or frame.

Cut all panels from 18 mm birch ply, guiding the jigsaw along a straight batten. Assemble the carcase with PVA glue and 40 mm screws, pre-drilling and countersinking each joint. Check the box is square by measuring the diagonals: equal diagonals mean a square box. Clamp with G-cramps or belt cramp if available while the glue sets. Fix the back panel last to lock the box square.
Locate studs and fit the wall fixing
Use a stud finder or probe with a bradawl to locate the wall studs or, on masonry, mark suitable rawlplug fixing positions. A

gives a clean, adjustable fixing for a heavy unit: bevel-rip two lengths of 18 mm ply at 45 degrees, fix one to the wall into studs or wall plugs, and screw the other to the back of the carcase. Check the wall cleat is level before fixing.

Hook the carcase over the wall cleat and check it sits level. Add two discreet screws through the bottom back edge of the carcase into the wall to prevent the unit from tipping forward in use. Sand all exposed ply faces progressively to 180 grit. Apply two coats of hardwax oil or tinted paint. Iron-on edge banding on the ply edges gives a clean finish without visible laminate layers.

attrs.symptom: The assembled box is not square: one diagonal is longer than the other
attrs.cause: The carcase was not held square while the glue set, or one panel was cut slightly out of square.
attrs.fix: While the glue is still wet, apply clamps diagonally across the longer diagonal to pull it square. Check with a try square at each corner.

attrs.symptom: Unit tips forward from the wall after hanging
attrs.cause: The french cleat on the carcase sits too high on the carcase back, pushing the top of the unit away from the wall.
attrs.fix: Reposition the carcase cleat lower so the unit hangs with its back flush against the wall. Add two small screws at the bottom back to secure it.
